entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9289"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 50</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Isa.50.1-Isa.50.11">Is 50:1-11</reference>. The Judgments on Israel Were Provoked by Their Crimes, yet They Are Not Finally Cast Off by God.</title> <div sID="gen15908" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9289"/><hi type="bold">1. Where ... mothers divorcement--</hi>Zion is "the mother"; the Jews are the children; and God the Husband and Father (<reference osisRef="Isa.54.5">Is 54:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.62.5">62:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.3.14">Jr 3:14</reference>). Gesenius thinks that God means by the question to deny that He had given "a bill of divorcement" to her, as was often done on slight pretexts by a husband (<reference osisRef="Deut.24.1">De 24:1</reference>), or that He had "sold" His and her "children," as a poor parent sometimes did (<reference osisRef="Exod.21.7">Ex 21:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.1">2Ki 4:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.5.5">Ne 5:5</reference>) under pressure of his "creditors"; that it was they who sold themselves through their own sins. Maurer explains, "Show the bill of your mother's divorcement, whom ... ; produce the creditors to whom ye have been sold; so it will be seen that it was not from any caprice of Mine, but through your own fault, your mother has been put away, and you sold" (<reference osisRef="Isa.52.3">Is 52:3</reference>). Horsley best explains (as the antithesis between "I" and "yourselves" shows, though Lowth translates, "Ye are sold") I have never given your mother a regular bill of divorcement; I have merely "put her away" for a time, and can, therefore, by right as her husband still take her back on her submission; I have not made you, the children, over to any "creditor" to satisfy a debt; I therefore still have the right of a father over you, and can take you back on repentance, though as rebellious children you have sold yourselves to sin and its penalty (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.21.25">1Ki 21:25</reference>).<div eID="gen15908" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15909" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bill ... whom--</hi>rather, "the bill with which I have put her away" [Maurer]. <div eID="gen15909" type="x-p"/>

Gesenius thinks that God means by the question to deny that He had given "a bill of divorcement" to her, as was often done on slight pretexts by a husband ( De 24:1 ), or that He had "sold" His and her "children," as a poor parent sometimes did ( Ex 21:7 ; 2Ki 4:1 ; Ne 5:5 ) under pressure of his "creditors"; that it was they who sold themselves through their own sins. Maurer explains, "Show the bill of your mother's divorcement, whom ... ; produce the creditors to whom ye have been sold; so it will be seen that it was not from any caprice of Mine, but through your own fault, your mother has been put away, and you sold" ( Is 52:3 ). Horsley best explains (as the antithesis between "I" and "yourselves" shows, though Lowth translates, "Ye are sold") I have never given your mother a regular bill of divorcement; I have merely "put her away" for a time, and can, therefore, by right as her husband still take her back on her submission; I have not made you, the children, over to any "creditor" to satisfy a debt; I therefore still have the right of a father over you, and can take you back on repentance, though as rebellious children you have sold yourselves to sin and its penalty ( 1Ki 21:25 ). bill ... whom-- rather, "the bill with which I have put her away" [Maurer].

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9292"/><div sID="gen15918" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9292"/>4. Messiah, as "the servant of Jehovah" (<reference osisRef="Isa.42.1">Is 42:1</reference>), declares that the office has been assigned to Him of encouraging the "weary" exiles of Israel by "words in season" suited to their case; and that, whatever suffering it is to cost Himself, He does not shrink from it (<reference osisRef="Isa.50.5">Is 50:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.50.6">6</reference>), for that He knows His cause will triumph at last (<reference osisRef="Isa.50.7">Is 50:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.50.8">8</reference>).<div eID="gen15918" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15919" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">learned--</hi>not in mere human learning, but in divinely taught modes of instruction and eloquence (<reference osisRef="Isa.49.2">Is 49:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.4.11">Ex 4:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.7.28">Mt 7:28</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.7.29">29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.13.54">13:54</reference>).<div eID="gen15919" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15920" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">speak a word in season--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Prov.15.23">Pr 15:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.25.11">25:11</reference>). Literally, "to succor by words," namely, in their season of need, the "weary" dispersed ones of Israel (<reference osisRef="Deut.28.65-Deut.28.67">De 28:65-67</reference>). Also, the spiritual "weary" (<reference osisRef="Isa.42.3">Is 42:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.11.28">Mt 11:28</reference>).<div eID="gen15920" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15921" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wakeneth morning by morning, &c.--</hi>Compare "daily rising up early" (<reference osisRef="Jer.7.25">Jr 7:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mark.1.35">Mr 1:35</reference>). The image is drawn from a master wakening his pupils early for instruction.<div eID="gen15921" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15922" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wakeneth ... ear--</hi>prepares me for receiving His divine instructions.<div eID="gen15922" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15923" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as the learned--</hi>as one taught by Him. He "learned obedience," experimentally, "by the things which He suffered"; thus gaining that practical learning which adapted Him for "speaking a word in season" to suffering men (<reference osisRef="Heb.5.8">He 5:8</reference>). <div eID="gen15923" type="x-p"/>

Literally fulfilled (<reference osisRef="Matt.27.26">Mt 27:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.26.27">26:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.18.33">Lu 18:33</reference>). To "pluck the hair" is the highest insult that can be offered an Oriental (<reference osisRef="2Sam.10.4">2Sa 10:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.3.30">La 3:30</reference>). (Compare "deal," or "proper," <reference osisRef="Isa.52.13">Is 52:13</reference>, Margin; <reference osisRef="Isa.53.10">Is 53:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.118.6">Psa 118:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.23.5">Jr 23:5</reference>).<div eID="gen15933" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15934" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as a garment--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.51.6">Is 51:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.51.8">8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.102.26">Psa 102:26</reference>). In contrast to the godly (<reference osisRef="Isa.50.10">Is 50:10</reference>), the wicked, in times of darkness, instead of trusting in God, trust in themselves (kindle a light for themselves to walk by) (<reference osisRef="Eccl.11.9">Ec 11:9</reference>). In exact proportion to mystic Babylon's previous "glorifying" of herself shall be her sorrow (<reference osisRef="Matt.25.30">Mt 25:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.8.12">8:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.18.7">Re 18:7</reference>). <chapter eID="Isa.50"/>
entries.content_plain: 11. In contrast to the godly ( Is 50:10 ), the wicked, in times of darkness, instead of trusting in God, trust in themselves (kindle a light for themselves to walk by) ( Ec 11:9 ). The image is continued from Is 50:10 , "darkness"; human devices for salvation ( Pr 19:21 ; 16:9 , 25 ) are like the spark that goes out in an instant in darkness (compare Job 18:6 ; 21:17 , with Psa 18:28 ). sparks-- not a steady light, but blazing sparks extinguished in a moment. walk-- not a command, but implying that as surely as they would do so, they should lie down in sorrow ( Jr 3:25 ). In exact proportion to mystic Babylon's previous "glorifying" of herself shall be her sorrow ( Mt 25:30 ; 8:12 ; Re 18:7 ).
